questions.q: In the book's opening definition, acute diarrhoea lasting no more than two weeks is considered:
opts: Protozoal until an organism is identified
Non-infectious unless a stool culture is positive
Inflammatory only when blood is visible
questions.exp: Acute diarrhoea (≤2 weeks) is considered infectious unless proved otherwise. (Book p46)

questions.q: Which duration boundary is used in the opening definition of acute diarrhoea?
questions.exp: The introductory definition uses acute diarrhoea of ≤2 weeks. (Book p46)

questions.q: The first classification diagram organizes infectious diarrhoea by:
questions.exp: The first diagram is headed 'Based on duration and severity'. (Book p46)

questions.q: A brief episode is placed in the diagram's benign, short-lasting, self-limiting branch. Which class is written at its end?
questions.exp: The <1-week benign, short-lasting, self-limiting branch ends in viral diarrhoea. (Book p46)

questions.q: In the same duration diagram, the <1-week episode marked 'complicated' leads to which broad cause?
questions.exp: The complicated <1-week branch is labelled bacterial. (Book p46)

questions.q: The diagram associates diarrhoea lasting more than one week with which broad group?
questions.exp: The >1-week branch in the duration diagram is labelled protozoal. (Book p46)

questions.q: The site-based classification distinguishes small bowel, large bowel, and:
opts: Enterocolitis involving small and large bowel
questions.exp: The third site category is enterocolitis (small bowel + large bowel). (Book p46)

questions.q: In the site classification, Yersinia is singled out for causing:
questions.exp: Yersinia is listed under enterocolitis and causes severe ileocolitis. (Book p46)

questions.q: Right-lower-quadrant tenderness during Yersinia ileocolitis is emphasized because it can mimic:
questions.exp: The note states that severe Yersinia ileocolitis produces right-lower-quadrant tenderness and mimics appendicitis. (Book p46)

questions.q: Which stool pattern best fits the small-bowel column on the clinical-features table?
opts: Large-volume watery stool without blood, pus or mucus
Painless formed stool streaked with blood
Frequent stools with fecal leukocytes and mucus
Small-volume bloody stool with urgency and tenesmus
questions.exp: Small-bowel diarrhoea is described as large-volume and watery, without blood, pus, mucus, increased frequency, urgency or tenesmus. (Book p46)

questions.q: A patient has small-volume bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes. The table localizes this pattern to the:
questions.exp: Fever, small-volume bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes are in the large-bowel column. (Book p46)

questions.q: Match each stool pattern to its site — 1) Large-volume watery stool without blood, pus or mucus 2) Small-volume bloody stool with fecal leukocytes … A) Large bowel B) Small bowel
questions.exp: The table places large-volume watery non-bloody stool in small-bowel disease and small-volume bloody stool with fecal leukocytes in large-bowel disease. (Book p46)

questions.q: Among adults, which virus is marked as the most common cause in the small-bowel column?
questions.exp: Norovirus is marked most common in adults. (Book p46)

questions.q: The virus marked most common in children is:
questions.exp: Rotavirus is marked most common in children. (Book p46)

questions.q: A post-transplant patient develops sore throat, diarrhoea and leucopenia. Which virus is named beside this presentation?
questions.exp: The page associates post-transplant CMV with sore throat, diarrhoea and leucopenia. (Book p46)

questions.q: The table places cytomegalovirus more prominently in which site?
opts: Small bowel rather than large bowel
Equal involvement of small and large bowel
Large bowel rather than small bowel
questions.exp: The printed comparison is cytomegalovirus (large bowel > small bowel). (Book p46)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the site table places fecal leukocytes with the large-bowel pattern, not the large-volume watery small-bowel pattern.
opts: True — fecal leukocytes are in the large-bowel column
False — the table does not mention fecal leukocytes
False — fecal leukocytes are listed only for small bowel
True — but the small-bowel stool is also described as bloody
questions.exp: Fecal leukocytes are listed in the large-bowel column; small-bowel stool is large-volume and watery without blood, pus or mucus. (Book p46)

questions.q: The small-bowel bacterial mechanism described as in-vivo toxin production raises which second messenger before secretory diarrhoea?
questions.exp: The table links in-vivo toxin production to increased cAMP and secretory diarrhoea. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which organism is labelled the most common small-bowel in-vivo secretory-toxin cause?
questions.exp: ETEC is marked most common under small-bowel in-vivo toxin production. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which second organism is listed alongside ETEC under small-bowel in-vivo toxin production?
questions.exp: The listed small-bowel in-vivo toxin producers are ETEC and Vibrio cholerae. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which set is grouped as preformed-toxin food poisoning in the small-bowel bacteria column?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens
Shigella flexneri, Campylobacter and non-typhoid Salmonella
questions.exp: The preformed-toxin group contains Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus and Clostridium perfringens. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which organism is listed as an invasive large-bowel bacterium and is linked to shigellosis?
questions.exp: Shigella flexneri is listed among invasive organisms in the large-bowel column and causes shigellosis. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which complete group lists the invasive bacteria named in the large-bowel column?
opts: Shigella flexneri, V. parahaemolyticus, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella and EIEC
ETEC, V. cholerae and Staphylococcus aureus
questions.exp: The complete large-bowel invasive list includes Shigella, V. parahaemolyticus, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella and EIEC. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which Vibrio species appears in the large-bowel invasive-organism list rather than the small-bowel secretory list?
questions.exp: V. parahaemolyticus is listed among large-bowel invasive organisms; V. cholerae is in the small-bowel secretory group. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which protozoal distribution matches the table?
opts: Small bowel: Entamoeba; large bowel: Giardia and Cryptosporidium
Small bowel: Entamoeba and microsporidium; large bowel: Cryptosporidium
Small bowel: Cryptosporidium, microsporidium, Giardia; large bowel: Entamoeba histolytica
Small bowel: Giardia only; large bowel: all other protozoa
questions.exp: The table lists Cryptosporidium, microsporidium and Giardia in small bowel; Entamoeba histolytica in large bowel. (Book p47)

questions.q: The note distinguishes Salmonella typhi from diarrhoeal small-bowel pathogens because small-bowel invasion is associated with:
opts: Fever with chills and abdominal pain, without diarrhoea
questions.exp: The note describes typhoid small-bowel invasion as fever with chills and abdominal pain, with no diarrhoea. (Book p47)

questions.q: Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning is caused by a:
opts: Shiga-like cytotoxin produced in the colon
questions.exp: The page labels the Staphylococcus aureus toxin preformed and heat stable. (Book p47)

questions.q: The incubation period written for Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning is:
questions.exp: The printed incubation period is 1–6 hours. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which source is specifically included in the Staphylococcus aureus food-poisoning list?
questions.exp: The listed sources are custard, pork and canned meat. (Book p47)

questions.q: After a shared meal, the earliest and most prominent symptom is vomiting. The page attributes this prominent symptom in S. aureus food poisoning to stimulation of:
questions.exp: Vomiting is the most prominent clinical feature and is attributed to 5-HT3 stimulation. (Book p47)

questions.q: Besides prominent vomiting, the other clinical feature listed for S. aureus food poisoning is:
questions.exp: The listed clinical features are vomiting and abdominal cramps. (Book p47)

questions.q: Which set reproduces the organisms listed as heat-stable-enterotoxin producers in the note?
opts: S. aureus, B. cereus, C. perfringens, Yersinia and E. coli
V. cholerae, Shigella, Campylobacter, Giardia and CMV
EIEC, EHEC, S. typhi, Rotavirus and Entamoeba
S. aureus, V. cholerae, EIEC, norovirus and CMV
questions.exp: The note lists S. aureus, B. cereus, C. perfringens, Yersinia and E. coli as producers of heat-stable enterotoxin. (Book p47)

questions.q: In the B. cereus table, which pairing is correct for the heat-stable toxin?
opts: Preformed toxin; 6–12 h; diarrhoea; raw fish
Formed toxin; 6–12 h; diarrhoea; meat and pudding
Preformed toxin; 1–6 h incubation; vomiting; undercooked fried rice
Formed toxin; 1–6 h; vomiting; canned meat
questions.exp: The heat-stable B. cereus toxin is preformed; incubation is 1–6 hours, vomiting predominates, and undercooked fried rice is the source. (Book p48)

questions.q: Which B. cereus table entry belongs to the heat-labile toxin?
opts: Preformed toxin with 1–6 h incubation and vomiting
Cytotoxic toxin with a 2-day incubation and pseudomembranes
Formed toxin with 6–12 h incubation and diarrhoea associated with increased cAMP
Shiga toxin with 6–72 h incubation and haemolysis
questions.exp: The heat-labile B. cereus toxin is formed; the table gives 6–12 hours and diarrhoea with increased cAMP. (Book p48)

questions.q: Which foods are listed as sources for the heat-labile B. cereus presentation?
questions.exp: The heat-labile B. cereus column lists meat, pudding and dried potato. (Book p48)

questions.q: The incubation period paired with formed, heat-labile B. cereus toxin is:
questions.exp: The table gives 6–12 hours for heat-labile B. cereus toxin. (Book p48)

questions.q: A diner eats undercooked fried rice and develops vomiting within a few hours. Which B. cereus toxin pattern fits the page?
questions.exp: Undercooked fried rice, vomiting and 1–6-hour incubation identify the preformed heat-stable B. cereus pattern. (Book p48)

questions.q: Vibrio cholerae is described as:
opts: A protozoan restricted to the colon
An organism that invades all four bowel-wall layers
questions.exp: The pathogenesis section labels V. cholerae non-invasive. (Book p48)

questions.q: The cholera enterotoxin increases secretion by activating:
questions.exp: The book states that the cholera enterotoxin activates adenyl cyclase. (Book p48)

questions.q: The toxin-coregulated pilus of V. cholerae mediates:
questions.exp: The toxin-coregulated pilus is described as mediating attachment to intestinal mucosa. (Book p48)

questions.q: A patient with cholera has profuse watery stool and marked volume depletion. Which stool-volume pattern is specifically listed?
opts: Formed stool with streaks of blood
questions.exp: The listed cholera features are large-volume watery diarrhoea and dehydration. (Book p48)

questions.q: The acid–base/electrolyte disturbance listed with cholera is:
questions.exp: The book lists hypokalaemic acidosis with a normal anion gap. (Book p48)

questions.q: For fluid replacement in the cholera treatment list, which fluid is named as the fluid of choice?
questions.exp: Ringer lactate is labelled the fluid of choice. (Book p48)

questions.q: Which antibiotic is named as the drug of choice for cholera in the book, with a pregnancy alternative also listed?
questions.exp: The printed drug of choice is doxycycline; azithromycin is listed in pregnancy. These are book-study notes, not current treatment guidance. (Book p48)

questions.q: Raw fish is the source listed for:
questions.exp: The V. parahaemolyticus section lists raw fish as the source. (Book p48)

questions.q: The named diagnostic phenomenon for V. parahaemolyticus is:
questions.exp: Kanagawa phenomenon is the listed diagnostic clue. (Book p48)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the V. parahaemolyticus section says acute diarrhoea may occur and antibiotics have no role.
opts: False — it causes chronic steatorrhoea and antibiotics are mandatory
True — acute diarrhoea is listed and antibiotics have no role
False — raw fish is not a listed source
True — but only when Kanagawa testing is negative
questions.exp: The page lists acute diarrhoea, Kanagawa phenomenon for diagnosis, and no role for antibiotics. (Book p48)

questions.q: ETEC is identified as the most common cause of:
questions.exp: ETEC is called the most common cause of community-acquired diarrhoea and travellers' diarrhoea. (Book p48)

questions.q: The ETEC toxin begun at the bottom of p48 is the heat-labile toxin, which raises:
questions.exp: The ETEC heat-labile toxin is linked to increased cAMP. (Book p48)

questions.q: The clinical feature used to introduce childhood HUS is the combination of:
questions.exp: The margin defines the HUS feature as haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia. (Book p49)

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of childhood HUS is assigned to the first branch on p49?
questions.exp: The diagram divides childhood HUS into 90% and 10% branches. (Book p49)

questions.q: The organism marked most common in the 90% childhood-HUS branch is:
questions.exp: EHEC O157:H7 is marked most common in the 90% branch. (Book p49)

questions.q: The toxin paired with EHEC O157:H7 is:
questions.exp: EHEC O157:H7 is paired with Shiga-like toxin, also called verocytotoxin. (Book p49)

questions.q: Which organism-toxin pair is also included in the 90% childhood-HUS branch?

questions.q: The p49 diagram assigns what proportion of childhood HUS to Streptococcus pneumoniae?
questions.exp: The S. pneumoniae branch is labelled 10%. (Book p49)

questions.q: The toxin named beside S. pneumoniae in the childhood-HUS diagram is:
questions.exp: The 10% S. pneumoniae branch is paired with neuraminidase toxin. (Book p49)

questions.q: The note distinguishes the heat-stable ETEC toxin from LT by linking it to increased:

questions.q: In the Shigella pathogenesis diagram, the invasive branch begins with:

questions.q: The invasive Shigella process is noted to affect how many layers of the intestinal wall?
questions.exp: The note says plasmid-antigen invasion affects all four layers of the intestinal wall. (Book p49)

questions.q: The invasive Shigella pathway is linked to severe inflammatory diarrhoea and:

questions.q: The toxin-mediated Shigella branches are paired as:

questions.exp: The diagram links enterotoxin with diarrhoea and Shiga-like toxin with cytotoxicity. (Book p49)

questions.q: Which drug is labelled the drug of choice for Shigella on p49?
questions.exp: Ciprofloxacin is labelled DOC; azithromycin is also listed as treatment. This reflects the book's study content, not current prescribing guidance. (Book p49)

questions.q: Which additional antibiotic is listed after ciprofloxacin in the Shigella treatment section?
questions.exp: Azithromycin is listed alongside ciprofloxacin for Shigella in the source. (Book p49)

questions.q: A patient with diarrhoea and arthritis is being distinguished from IBD. The note says IBD can be identified by fecal:

questions.q: Which extraintestinal feature is specifically included in that IBD differential note?
questions.exp: The note's extraintestinal list includes erythema nodosum, episcleritis and type-I peripheral arthritis. (Book p49)

questions.q: The non-typhoid Salmonella source is described as:
questions.exp: Non-typhoid Salmonella is listed as faeco-oral. (Book p49)

questions.q: The incubation interval listed for non-typhoid Salmonella is:
questions.exp: The p49 incubation period is 6–72 hours. (Book p49)

questions.q: The pathogenesis phrase used for non-typhoid Salmonella is:

questions.q: The complication singled out as the most severe in non-typhoid Salmonella is:
questions.exp: Aortoarteritis is marked as the most severe complication; endovascular infection is also listed. (Book p49)

questions.q: Besides aortoarteritis, which complication is listed for non-typhoid Salmonella?
questions.exp: Endovascular infection is the second listed complication. (Book p49)

questions.q: In the Salmonella typhi note, diarrhoea in enteric fever is placed in which week?

questions.exp: The note says enteric fever has diarrhoea in the second week. (Book p50)

questions.q: The common complication named for typhoid in the p50 note is:

questions.q: Which haematologic complication is included in the Salmonella typhi note?

questions.q: Which gastrointestinal complication is listed alongside typhoid perforation?

questions.q: The photograph on p50 is captioned:

questions.q: Campylobacter jejuni is acquired by the route listed as:
questions.exp: The C. jejuni source is faeco-oral. (Book p50)

questions.q: The incubation period listed for C. jejuni is:

questions.q: C. jejuni is listed as a risk factor for which later disease category?
questions.exp: The complication list names inflammatory bowel disease as a risk association. (Book p50)

questions.q: The neurological syndrome C. jejuni is said to trigger is:

questions.q: Which age threshold appears among the C. jejuni management indications?

questions.q: The stool-frequency threshold listed among the management indications is:
questions.exp: The source gives ≥6 stools/day. (Book p50)

questions.exp: The listed culture targets are Shigella, Salmonella and Campylobacter. (Book p50)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the page groups stool culture and azithromycin treatment as not routinely indicated in small-bowel diarrhoea.
opts: True — the brace marks both as not routinely indicated in small-bowel diarrhoea
False — the brace applies only to culture
False — the brace applies only to azithromycin
True — but only for large-bowel diarrhoea

questions.q: The azithromycin dose shown in the C. jejuni management note is:
questions.exp: The page lists azithromycin 500 mg; it is book-study content rather than a prescribing recommendation. (Book p50)

questions.q: The p50 section heading for the next disorder is:
questions.exp: The next heading is pseudomembranous enterocolitis. (Book p50)

questions.q: The organism named under pseudomembranous-enterocolitis pathogenesis is:
questions.exp: The pathogenesis section names C. difficile. (Book p50)

questions.q: The page links antibiotic exposure in C. difficile pathogenesis to a change in:

questions.q: Which toxin description is correct for C. difficile on p50?
opts: Toxin A is an enterotoxin; toxin B is cytotoxic and the most potent
Toxin A is cytotoxic and most potent; toxin B is an enterotoxin

questions.q: The incubation period printed for pseudomembranous enterocolitis is:
questions.exp: The page gives an incubation period of 2 days. (Book p50)

Only formed stool streaked with blood

questions.q: The stool pattern in the C. difficile clinical-features section is categorized as:

questions.q: The major complication illustrated and named for C. difficile enterocolitis is:

questions.q: The relative order of toxic-megacolon associations printed in parentheses is:

Pseudomembranous enterocolitis > invasive infection > ulcerative colitis
Pseudomembranous enterocolitis > ulcerative colitis > invasive-organism infection

questions.q: When both the GDH test and toxin EIA are positive, the diagram concludes:

questions.q: The page notes that oral fidaxomicin has which advantage in the non-severe branch?

questions.exp: A downward arrow and 'recurrence' are noted beside oral fidaxomicin. (Book p51)

questions.q: Which additional oral antibiotic is listed for non-severe C. difficile disease?
questions.exp: Oral vancomycin is listed beside fidaxomicin in the non-severe branch. (Book p51)

questions.q: A patient has WBC >15,000 and creatinine >1.5 but no ileus, shock or megacolon. Which category does the flowchart use?

questions.q: Which dose of oral fidaxomicin is specified in the severe branch?

questions.q: Which other oral agent appears in the severe C. difficile branch?

questions.q: Which combination is listed for fulminant C. difficile disease?

Oral vancomycin, IV metronidazole and surgical consultation
Doxycycline, Ringer lactate and no surgical input

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — in the p51 flowchart, fulminant disease adds IV metronidazole and surgical consultation to oral vancomycin.
opts: True — all three appear in the fulminant branch
False — IV metronidazole is listed for non-severe disease
True — but vancomycin is not included
questions.exp: The fulminant branch lists oral vancomycin, IV metronidazole and surgical consultation. (Book p51)

units.title: Definitions & Site Patterns
units.guide:
Acute diarrhoea ≤2 weeks is infectious unless proved otherwise.
Duration branches: <1 week benign/viral or complicated/bacterial; >1 week protozoal.
Separate small-bowel large-volume watery stool from large-bowel small-volume bloody stool.

units.title: Small- and Large-Bowel Organisms
units.guide:
Small bowel: ETEC/V. cholerae toxins, preformed-toxin bacteria, Cryptosporidium, microsporidium, Giardia.
Large bowel: Shigella, Campylobacter, non-typhoid Salmonella, EIEC, V. parahaemolyticus, Entamoeba.
Typhoid is a small-bowel invasion with fever/pain and no diarrhoea in the note.

units.title: Preformed-Toxin Food Poisoning
units.guide:
S. aureus: preformed heat-stable toxin, 1–6 h, custard/pork/canned meat, vomiting via 5-HT3.
B. cereus heat-stable: fried rice/vomiting; heat-labile: formed toxin, 6–12 h, diarrhoea/cAMP.
The source also lists Yersinia and E. coli among heat-stable-toxin producers.

units.title: Vibrio, ETEC & Secretory Diarrhoea
units.guide:
V. cholerae is non-invasive; toxin activates adenyl cyclase; TCP attaches to mucosa.
Large-volume watery stool, dehydration and hypokalaemic normal-gap acidosis; the page names Ringer lactate.
V. parahaemolyticus: raw fish/Kanagawa; ETEC LT raises cAMP and is linked to travellers' diarrhoea.

units.title: HUS and Shigella
units.guide:
Childhood HUS: 90% EHEC O157:H7/Shigella dysenteriae toxins; 10% pneumococcal neuraminidase.
Shigella invasion affects all four bowel-wall layers; enterotoxin causes diarrhoea and Shiga-like toxin is cytotoxic.
The note contrasts diarrhoea with arthritis against IBD markers and extraintestinal signs.

units.title: Salmonella and Campylobacter
units.guide:
Typhoid: diarrhoea in week two, perforation, marrow suppression and intestinal bleeding.
C. jejuni is faeco-oral, incubates 2–4 days, and is linked to IBD, GBS and IPSID/lymphoma.
The page's culture and azithromycin notes are explicitly not routine for small-bowel diarrhoea.

units.title: C. difficile Enterocolitis
units.guide:
GDH + toxin A/B EIA → confirm if both positive; discordant results go to PCR/NAAT.
The p51 flowchart separates non-severe, severe and fulminant disease by WBC/creatinine and ileus/shock/megacolon.
Treatment entries reproduce the book for study; they are not current clinical guidance.
